text: Caspa's core contributors just moved their first token standard KCC20 into its final review window. On October 7th, 2026, pull request 31 merges into Caspa's own conventions repo and the status on the spec flips to last call, the final review window before standard goes final. Real tokens on Caspa's base layer with every transaction enforced by the chain's own script rules, not by an off chain indexer. Real, close, not yet finished. So let's get into how this is all playing out. Start with where this comes from. On June 30th, 2026, the Tokata hard fork gave Caspa covenants. A covenant is a rule built into a coin that controls how it is spent and where it can go next. KCC20 is the shared rule book for a fungible token built from those covenants. Fungible meaning every unit is the same as every other. Four ideas. Idea 1. A common interface. Every KCC20 token carries the same state block, the amount, the owner, a few settings, and the same transfer or entry point. So any wallet, indexer, or app reads it the same way. Idea 2. Extended state. A token can carry its own data and behavior behind one digest. And transfers pass that digest through, untouched. Idea 3. Flexible authority. And this comes from KCC2. The owner of a token can be a public key, a key commitment, a script, or another covenant. So covenants can own tokens and govern them. Idea 4. Borrowed receive. Here's the thing. Every UTXO, every unspent coin, has to be funded with CAS. And a rule called storage mass makes tiny outputs expensive on purpose. So instead of a UTXO for every incoming token, the sender tops up one you already hold. Same owner, the CAS inside cannot go down, only the token amount grows. Now, CASPA already has tokens, KRC20, from CASPLEX, a third-party control, live since September 2024. Around 2160 tokens by CASPLEX's own indexer account. It proved the demand. The difference is where the token lives. With KRC20, token operations are written onto CASPA as data, and the CASPLEX indexer works out who owns that. Your balance is the indexer's answer. With KCC20, the token state sits inside a covenant UTXO on the base layer, and the chain script enforces every transfer. Your balance is what the chain enforces. Sivan Helfer, the first listed author of KCC20, put it plainly back in June, a week before Tokata went live. That is the whole difference. On the KCC20 side, it is very early. Roughly 150 tokens by one community's tracker account. Think ERC20, enforced by the base layer itself. The timeline, straight from the repo. June 30th, Tokata activates. July 15th, the convention repo opens. August 20th, KCC1, KCC2, and KCC20 land as drabs. On September 22nd, the Last Call pull request for KCC20 opens. October 1st, KCC1, KCC2 move to Last Call. October 7th, KCC20 joins them. Last Call is the final review window. An editor sets a deadline, typically around 14 days out, but none of the three headers carries one today, no official end date. And KCC20 cannot go final on its own. It requires KCC1, the Covenant layout, and KCC2, the authority schemes. And those go final first. KCC1, and then KCC2, then KCC20. It also needs published test vectors and a public implementation that passes them. Today, the number of final technical standards in that repo is zero. By late July, implementers were already reporting that their tokens only partly mashed a draft. So what's the bigger picture? Let's zoom out. After the September 22nd release, the main node code went quiet for three weeks. Then SIX commits landing in one week, October 13th to the 16th. Maintenance and plumbing, not a new feature. And DagNight, the next consensus upgrade, still has no date. Usage is a tiny base, around 82,000 standard transactions a day the week of October, up around 22% on the week before. So here's the conditional case. If KCC1, KCC2, then KCC20 go final, every wallet, indexer, and app on CASPA builds to one rulebook. Tokens exist today. That shared standard does not, yet. And the supply is fixed. Proof of work, no pre-mine. Around 96.7% of all CASPA is already mined. New demand meets very little new supply. Conditional, and that's the asymmetry I'm watching.
